cues.text: A Troubled Marriage
In 1427, in the city of Zaragoza, Spain, a married woman whose husband treated her harshly consulted a local sorcerer for a remedy that might soften his temper.
The sorcerer told her the charm he had in mind required a consecrated Host, and instructed her to obtain one.
A Host Concealed and Burned

The woman went to the church of St. Michael, made her confession, and received Communion — then, rather than consuming the Host, concealed it and carried it home in a small coffer, exactly as the sorcerer had directed.

When the sorcerer opened the coffer, both were startled to find not a Host but an infant, glowing with light, in its place; he instructed her to burn the Eucharist to ashes and bring them back to him.
She did as told, but when the coffer was opened again, the coffer itself had burned completely while the child inside remained entirely untouched.
Brought Before the Bishop
Overcome with fear and remorse, the woman brought the coffer and its contents to Bishop Alonso de Arguello.
He had the child placed under guard on the altar of St. Valerius in the cathedral.
The people of Zaragoza came throughout the following day to see and venerate what they had been told was a visible sign of Christ's presence.
A Host at the Altar
The next morning, as the bishop celebrated the Votive Mass of the Blessed Sacrament at that same altar, the figure of the child vanished at the offertory.
In its place, the congregation saw an already-consecrated Host, which the bishop, recognizing no further consecration was needed, distributed and himself received at Communion.
The event is recorded in a written account left by the city's archdeacon, Don Dorner, and preserved in Zaragoza's town hall archives.
A painting depicting the episode still hangs in the cathedral beside the chapel of San Dominguito del Val.
Legacy
According to the tradition, the woman was reconciled with her husband afterward and lived the rest of her life in evident devotion.

Whatever one makes of the story's more dramatic elements, this detail frames the whole account less as punishment than as a troubled marriage transformed by an encounter neither spouse could have anticipated.
The story remains part of Zaragoza's civic memory nearly six centuries later, preserved in both municipal archive and cathedral art.
